# Workflows from earlier work in this repository

Reusable steps learned from earlier tasks here. Values your task states are filled in; blanks in braces stand for the rest of your task's own names and values. Places are found in the code as it is now (current line numbers); the lines shown are excerpts.

## 1. Add a parameter to an existing rule
Filled from your task: {param} = `>`
Blanks: {rule_id} the existing rule's identifier; {rule_file} lowercase file name of the rule (module, doc); {alias} the existing rule's alias; {param_description} short description text used in docs and schema; {fixture_name} name of each new fixture file, named after the rule's existing fixtures
1. In the rule's own module lib/{rule_file}.mjs, read > from params.config with its default and implement the behaviour (report as before: same line and context). The existing module is a whole-file read; no other registration is needed.
2. Describe > in the doc body doc-build/{rule_file}.md (what it does, default), and mirror the same text in doc/{rule_file}.md (including a `- `>`: description (`type`, default `x`)` line in its Parameters list).
3. Add the same parameter line and body text to the rule's section in doc/Rules.md.
4. In the schema builder's existing case for the rule, add `subscheme.properties.>` with description, type and default (keep the `// @ts-ignore` comment style used by the neighbours).
   `schema/build-config-schema.mjs:92-717` in for (const rule of rules) { › switch (ruleName) {
   ```
      92|   switch (ruleName) {
        ⋮
     711|         },
     712|         "default": []
     713|       };
     714|       break;
     715|     default:
     716|       break;
     717|   }
   ```
5. Add > with its description comment and default to the rule's entry in the sample JSONC config and in the sample YAML config. (regeneration (`npm run build-config`) did not add it)
   `schema/.markdownlint.jsonc:2-377` in {
   ```
       2| {
        ⋮
     370|   },
     372|   // MD064/link-url-scheme : Link URL scheme should be allowed : https://github.com/DavidAnson/markdownlint/blob/v0.41.1/doc/md064.md
     373|   "MD064": {
     374|     // Allowed URL schemes (empty for all schemes)
     375|     "allowed_schemes": []
     376|   }
     377| }
   ```
6. Add the > property (description, type, default) in BOTH the strict and non-strict JSON schemas, and in each of them under BOTH the rule-id entry and the alias entry. Likewise add `>?: type;` with a doc comment under both the id and alias entries of the ConfigurationStrict typings. Prefer regenerating with `npm run build-config` and verifying the four-plus places.
   `schema/markdownlint-config-schema-strict.json:6-5496` in { › "properties": {
   ```
       6|   "properties": {
        ⋮
    5490|             "warning"
    5491|           ]
    5492|         }
    5493|       ],
    5494|       "default": true
    5495|     }
    5496|   },
   ```
7. In test/wrong-types-in-config-file.md, add > with a wrong-typed value inside the rule's alias config block.
8. Increase t.plan in the strict-schema validation test (observed +3 for one parameter, matching the added schema entries).
   `test/markdownlint-test.mjs:1096-1132` in test.suite(import.meta.url.replace(/^.*?\/(?<name>[^/]*)$/u, "$<nam... › test("validateJsonUsingConfigSchemaStrict", async(t) => {
   ```
    1096|   test("validateJsonUsingConfigSchemaStrict", async(t) => {
        ⋮
    1126|           !!result,
    1127|           true,
    1128|           `${file}\n${JSON.stringify(validateSchemaStrict.errors, null, 2)}`
    1129|         );
    1130|       }
    1131|     }
    1132|   });
   ```
9. Create fixtures test/{fixture_name}.md modelled on the rule's existing fixtures (a whole example fixture of the neighbouring kind is shown): one per behaviour, including combinations with other existing parameters, with `<!-- markdownlint-configure-file {...} -->` and `{{rule_id}:line}` annotations. Keep annotation line numbers matching the offending lines.
   a new file in `test/`, named like the 33 there that start with `heading`; shortest first: heading-multiple-top-level-preceding-blank.md (5 lines), heading-multiple-top-level-preceding-comment.md (5 lines), heading_increment-title_level3_bad.md (6 lines), headings_good.md (6 lines), heading-multiple-top-level-preceding-blank-and-comment.md (7 lines), heading_increment-title_level2_good.md (8 lines). The shortest, `test/heading-multiple-top-level-preceding-blank.md`:
   ```
       1| 
       2| # Heading 1
       3| 
       4| # Heading 2 {MD025}
   ```
10. Run `npm run update-snapshots`, check the snapshot diff only holds the new fixtures, then run the full test and lint.
Watch out: In test fixtures the `{RULE:line}` annotations must name the real line of the offending text; when annotations sit on their own lines they shift later lines, and wrong numbers make npm test fail on several fixtures at once. Count lines carefully (or run the fixture test first) before regenerating snapshots, and review the snapshot diff.
Watch out: After adding a rule or schema entries, several hard-coded counts in the tests (file counts and t.plan values in several tests) go stale; guessing increments or fixing only the first reported ones costs repeated slow full test runs. Update all count places at once and take exact values from the 'plan expected X but received Y' messages.

## Last: check it all with one command
When all your edits are in, run once: `npm run lint; npm run build-config; npm run build-docs; npm test; git status --short`
These are the checks earlier runs of these workflows passed, in one call. Its output is long: keep its last 60 lines (`2>&1 | tail -n 60` in Bash, `2>&1 | Select-Object -Last 60` in PowerShell), or Claude Code saves it to a file you then have to read.
In those runs the checks rewrote these test snapshots, as expected for this kind of change: `test/markdownlint-test-scenarios.mjs.snapshot`.
